nameStory: The word 'tomato' comes from the Nahuatl (Aztec) word 'tomatl,' which the Spanish explorers heard and adapted when they encountered this fruit in Central America. Interestingly, tomatoes were once called 'love apples' in Europe, possibly because the French called them 'pommes d'amour' - though whether this was for their supposed aphrodisiac properties or simply a mispronunciation is still debated!
description: The tomato is a sprawling, vine-like plant that most New Englanders know from their vegetable gardens. These tender annuals grow 2-6 feet tall with soft, hairy stems that need staking or caging for support. The familiar red, round fruits are actually berries botanically speaking, and the whole plant has a distinctive, sharp 'green' smell that rubs off on your hands when you brush against it.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: The classic round, red fruit (though varieties can be yellow, purple, or green) with smooth, shiny skin and multiple seed chambers inside filled with gel-like pulp

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large, compound leaves divided into 5-9 oval leaflets with smaller leaflets between the main ones, feeling slightly fuzzy and sticky to the touch

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small yellow flowers with 5 pointed petals that curve backward, growing in clusters and having a sweet, mild fragrance

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Sprawling vine that grows upward with support, with soft, hollow stems covered in fine hairs that feel slightly sticky when touched

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Distinctive sharp, 'green' vegetable smell when leaves or stems are crushed, immediately recognizable to most gardeners

habitat: In New England, tomatoes are found almost exclusively in cultivated gardens, farms, and occasionally as volunteers in compost piles or disturbed soil. They thrive in rich, well-drained soil in full sun locations, often in raised beds or containers. You might spot escaped plants growing wild near former garden sites, though they rarely survive New England winters.

seasonality.spring: Seeds are started indoors in March-April, with young plants featuring their characteristic compound leaves and that distinctive tomato plant smell when brushed against.
seasonality.summer: Plants are in full growth with yellow flowers blooming continuously and green fruits developing. This is prime identification season when both flowers and developing fruits are visible.
seasonality.fall: Fruits ripen to their final colors (usually red) and plants begin to decline with cooler weather, often showing yellowing lower leaves as harvest season peaks.
seasonality.winter: Plants are completely killed by frost in New England, leaving only dried brown stalks if not cleaned up from gardens.

funFact: Tomatoes can actually self-fertilize, but they produce sweeter, more flavorful fruit when bumblebees perform 'buzz pollination' - grabbing onto the flower and vibrating their flight muscles to shake loose more pollen than the plant could manage on its own!
confusionNotes: Young tomato plants are sometimes confused with potato plants (their close cousin), but potato leaves are more uniformly green and less sticky-feeling, and potatoes develop small white or purple flowers rather than yellow ones. Remember: yellow flowers and sticky leaves usually mean tomato!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being eaten as a vegetable, tomatoes are botanically fruits - specifically berries. They're also members of the nightshade family, making them relatives of both potatoes and the toxic plants like deadly nightshade, which is why tomato leaves and green parts of the fruit contain mild toxins and shouldn't be eaten.
compareHints: Among its nightshade relatives in New England, tomato is easily distinguished by its large, edible red fruit and cultivation in gardens. Wild nightshades like bittersweet nightshade have much smaller berries and different leaf shapes, while potato plants have white or purple flowers instead of yellow. The combination of yellow flowers, large red fruit, and sticky, compound leaves is unique to tomatoes among local nightshades.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike other nightshades in New England, bittersweet nightshade is the only one that grows as a climbing vine with purple flowers.
Among New England's nightshades, Carolina horsenettle is the only one covered in sharp prickles, making it instantly recognizable.
Unlike bittersweet nightshade which has purple flowers and grows as a climbing vine, eastern black nightshade has white flowers and grows as a low bushy annual.
Among New England nightshades, buffalo-bur is unmistakable due to its extreme spininess - no other Solanum species is nearly as heavily armed with spines.
Black nightshade differs from its cousin bittersweet nightshade by being much smaller and having white flowers instead of purple ones with swept-back petals.
Unlike its nightshade relatives, potato has compound leaves rather than simple ones, and produces edible underground tubers.
Hairy nightshade differs from eastern black nightshade by its distinctly hairy stems and leaves (black nightshade is mostly smooth).

Green nightshade stands apart from its New England nightshade relatives primarily by its persistently green, glossy berries - eastern black nightshade and black nightshade both produce dark purple-black berries when ripe, while bittersweet nightshade produces bright red berries.
Unlike its wild nightshade relatives that grow as weeds in New England, cultivated eggplant is much larger in all aspects - bigger leaves, bigger flowers, and dramatically bigger fruits.

Garden huckleberry differs from other nightshades in New England by its drooping clusters of dark berries and relatively benign nature – unlike bittersweet nightshade with its bright red berries, or the more weedy black nightshade species.
Unlike other nightshades in New England, red buffalo-bur is the most heavily armed with prickles covering every surface.
